related_questions.question: Which is the most common brain tumor?
related_questions.snippet: Meningioma. Meningioma is the most common primary brain tumor, accounting for more than 30% of all brain tumors. Meningiomas originate in the meninges, the outer three layers of tissue that cover and protect the brain just under the skull.

related_questions.question: What is the biggest symptom of a brain tumor?
related_questions.snippet: Headaches are the most common symptom of brain tumors. Headaches happen in about half of people with brain tumors. Headaches can happen if a growing brain tumor presses on healthy cells around it. Or a brain tumor can cause swelling in the brain that increases pressure in the head and leads to a headache.

related_questions.snippet: Glioblastoma: The deadliest form of brain cancer It is also the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults, though it can strike at any age. It can form in the spinal cord or the brain.
related_questions.title: Fighting glioblastoma - one of the deadliest forms of brain cancer

text_blocks.snippet: Brain tumors, whether primary (originating in the brain) or secondary (spreading from elsewhere), can manifest with a variety of symptoms that vary based on tumor location and size. Common symptoms include headaches, seizures, vision changes, and neurological deficits like weakness or numbness on one side of the body. Personality changes, cognitive difficulties, and balance problems can also occur.
snippet_highlighted_words: headaches, seizures, vision changes, and neurological deficits like weakness or numbness on one side of the body

list.title: Gliomas:
list.snippet: These are primary brain tumors that develop from glial cells, which support and protect nerve cells. They include astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, and ependymomas, among others.

list.title: Meningiomas:
list.snippet: These are typically benign tumors that arise from the meninges, the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

list.title: Pituitary Tumors:
list.snippet: These tumors can be benign or malignant and affect the pituitary gland, which regulates hormone production.

list.title: Metastatic Brain Tumors:
list.snippet: These are secondary tumors that spread to the brain from other parts of the body, such as the lungs, breast, or colon.

list.title: Medulloblastomas:
list.snippet: These are malignant tumors that originate in the cerebellum, the part of the brain that controls balance and coordination.

list.title: Pineal Region Tumors:
list.snippet: These tumors develop in or near the pineal gland, which produces melatonin.

list.title: Craniopharyngiomas:
list.snippet: These are benign tumors that develop near the pituitary gland.
Headaches: Can be persistent, worsening over time, and may be more severe in the morning or disrupt sleep.
Seizures: Can manifest as muscle spasms, convulsions, or altered awareness.
Vision Changes: Blurred vision, double vision, loss of peripheral vision, or even blindness in one or both eyes.
Neurological Deficits: Weakness, numbness, or paralysis on one side of the body, difficulty with balance, coordination, or speech.
Cognitive Changes: Memory loss, confusion, difficulty with thinking, concentration, or language.
Personality and Mood Changes: Irritability, changes in behavior, depression, or anxiety.
Other Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, fatigue, hearing loss, dizziness, and changes in appetite or weight.

text_blocks.snippet: Important Note: Brain tumor symptoms can be subtle and may resemble other conditions. Any new, persistent, or concerning symptoms should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.
